messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 73

He is 26, a Latin American man who now works as a maid in a downtown hotel, moving quietly through other people’s rooms with a cart of fresh towels and bleach. By the time he tells his story, he has been divorced for almost a year. He speaks carefully, often with long pauses, as if each memory must be handled without looking at it directly.

The trauma begins in his home country three years earlier. At the time, he is married and doing odd cleaning jobs in offices and private homes. He keeps mostly to himself. One evening, men in uniform stop him on his way home. He remembers the brightness of a flashlight in his face and how quickly ordinary life disappears. He is accused of helping people he does not know. When he denies it, they laugh. He is taken to a concrete room with no windows, where time loses shape. He does not tell the story in a straight line at first. Instead, he returns over several sessions to fragments: being forced to kneel for hours, the sting of water thrown on him when he starts to drift, a bag over his head that leaves him gasping and panicked, blows to his ribs and thighs, voices that ask the same questions again and again. What stays with him most is not only the pain but the helplessness. He says he learns very fast that the men can do anything they want and that his body no longer belongs to him.

After he is released, he goes home changed in ways that are immediately visible to his wife and in ways he tries to hide. He startles when doors shut. He sleeps in short bursts and wakes drenched in sweat, clawing at his throat. He does not want to be touched unexpectedly. At night he hears motorcycles outside and feels himself back in that room before he can remind himself where he is. His wife asks what happened, but he gives her only pieces. He feels ashamed of his fear and ashamed that he survived by begging. During the day he tries to return to work, but whenever a man raises his voice nearby, his vision narrows and his hands shake. In small bathrooms where he is supposed to scrub tile, he suddenly cannot breathe. He begins leaving jobs unfinished and inventing excuses.

The marriage starts to break under the weight of what he cannot say. His wife complains that he is absent even when sitting beside her. He becomes irritable, then guilty, then withdrawn. He checks the locks repeatedly and insists the curtains stay closed. He avoids friends and relatives because their questions feel dangerous. Crowded places make him scan every face for threat. He stops laughing. Sex becomes almost impossible; closeness brings back the feeling of being trapped in his own body. His wife interprets his distance as rejection, and he cannot find language that would make sense of the terror. Eventually they separate, and the divorce follows after he has already left the country for work.

Now, in the hotel, his job suits and torments him. He likes the predictability of cleaning: making a bed with crisp corners, lining up toiletries, wiping a mirror until no streak remains. Order calms him. But there are triggers everywhere. The housekeeping closet is narrow and windowless, and if the door swings shut behind him he feels a jolt of raw panic. The smell of bleach reminds him of the room where he was held. When guests leave the television on with loud shouting or news footage of police and soldiers, his stomach turns cold. If a supervisor comes up behind him unexpectedly, he drops what he is holding. He laughs it off, embarrassed, but afterwards his heart pounds for half an hour.

His nights are worse. He sleeps with the lights on or the television murmuring because silence feels unsafe. Even then he wakes from dreams in which he cannot breathe and someone is asking questions he cannot answer. Sometimes he sits on the side of the bed until morning, too afraid to sleep again. On his days off he tells himself he should explore the city or call family, but he often stays inside his apartment, exhausted and watchful. He drinks more than he wants to admit because for a few hours it dulls the memories, though the next day he feels more on edge.

He says the hardest part is that his life looks normal from the outside. At work he is known as reliable and meticulous. Guests rarely notice him except when a room is especially clean. But inside, he is living as if the danger has not ended. He studies exits in every building. He sits with his back to walls. He avoids men in uniform and crosses the street when he sees them. He carries himself with a constant tension, as though bracing for another blow. When he speaks about the torture, he does so with his eyes lowered, twisting a paper tissue between his fingers, and he seems surprised that his body still reacts as if those men are in the room with him now.
